title: By region and by table
standfirst: France rewards depth in one region and punishes the grand tour.

blocks.heading: Cellars, markets and one base
paras: The French countryside is a sequence of small regions that each take a week to understand and twenty minutes to drive across.
We choose one, put members in a house inside it, and build the week around the market days and two or three cellar visits.

blocks.heading: The cellars worth the detour
blocks.caption: Visits arranged with the makers, not the shops.
paras: The estates worth visiting do not take walk-ins and frequently do not have a tasting room at all.
Introductions are made months ahead, and the visits are with the person who makes the wine rather than with a guide.

blocks.heading: Alps in winter
blocks.caption: Chalets with their own staff rather than hotel suites.
paras: The French Alps in January are a different proposition entirely, and the good chalets go a year ahead.
We book winter in spring, which is the only way to get the ones with the right aspect and a proper kitchen.

blocks.heading: Questions members ask
blocks.intro: The ones that come up nearly every time.

a: May to October for the countryside and coast; December to March for the Alps.

items.q: Paris at the start or the end?
a: The start. It is the easiest arrival and the countryside is the better ending.
No, and we recommend members drive themselves in the countryside. A driver matters in the cities and on the arrival day.

blocks.heading: We are ready when you are
paras: Every itinerary starts with a conversation about what you actually want from the days, and works backwards to houses, guides and timing from there.
